extracted.intended_audience: ACL 2023 reviewers (general reviewers, area chairs, senior area chairs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for reviewing submissions to ACL 2023, covering how to write each review field, scoring (soundness vs excitement), reproducibility/ethics checks, and author-flagging procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial actions on assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Please have a look at the paper as soon as you get the assignment. If you notice any serious issues with the paper (format violations, missing compulsory sections, deanonymization through self-citations, acknowledgements or non-anonymous repositories), or you feel that the paper is too far out of your area of expertise, reach out to your senior area chair so that they can adjust the assignments or consider desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checking early can save work; if you only look at the paper close to the deadline, it will be too late.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper should be standalone
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission has to contain the actual paper, which may be accompanied by appendices, code and/or data. As a general rule, the paper should be readable as a standalone document, and any details important for understanding the key aspects of the work should be in the paper rather than in appendices, accompanying source code, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-key aspects (implementation details, parameters, examples or extra experiments) can be in supplementary materials and may be considered if you have questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is this paper about? (summary field)
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary of a paper should be a neutral, dispassionate summary of the research question and findings/contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge all contributions you believe the paper is making (experimental evidence, replication, framing a new question, artifacts, literature review, conceptual/theoretical arguments). State contributions in your own words rather than copy/pasting the abstract to show understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to accept (recognize strengths)
rubrics_metrics.description: List the paper's best aspects honestly even if you disagree with other parts. Contributions may be engineering solutions, literature reviews, useful artifacts, reproduction, analysis, theory, argumentation/position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the study advances the field (what did we learn/new capability). Performance improvements or complex math alone are neither necessary nor sufficient. If strength is performance, check baseline strength, robustness, computation budget reporting, and whether result reporting is honest (not cherry-picked). Consult Responsible NLP checklist or supplementary materials if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to reject (identify substantive weaknesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical problems include claims not supported by evidence/arguments, misleading framing, methodological flaws (e.g., only best-run reported), errors in proofs/implementation/analysis, insufficient detail to understand or reproduce, lack of clarity about research question, or not making clear how findings advance the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between true weaknesses and things that belong in 'suggestions'. Do not penalize honest, well-considered limitations (there is a mandatory limitations section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for the Author(s) (major questions only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve this section for big questions whose answers would be relevant for your recommendation; authors have limited space to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use letter numbering scheme (Question A:, Question B:, ...) and combine with reviewer number when referring in rebuttal/discussion (e.g., 2A). Do not use this for typos or minor issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing references (provide full citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: List any references that should be included in the bibliography or discussed in more depth. If claiming lack of novelty, give the specific work you believe is similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full citation entries when suggesting missing prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typos, grammar, style, presentation (authors-only field)
rubrics_metrics.description: This field is exclusively a message to the authors: presentation suggestions, clarifications, and a reasonable list of typos or language errors that do not count as 'weaknesses'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the paper is illegible or unclear, such issues can escalate to 'weaknesses' for the chairs. For substantive comments/questions for the authors, use the Questions field instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful suggesting self-citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful in suggesting citations of your own papers; when truly relevant it's appropriate but may de-anonymize the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A workaround is to suggest several citations including yours so as not to single out your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness (scoring dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soundness goes to how well the paper clearly states its claims and backs them up with evidence and argumentation; papers should clear a minimum bar for technically sound research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with fellow reviewers to reach consensus on the paper's claims and whether you believe them. Soundness expected to have lower variance across reviewers than excitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excitement (scoring dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excitement captures more subjective evaluations of novelty/significance and potential interest to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify your excitement score in text; disentangle excitement from soundness (a paper can be sound but not exciting). Explain reasoning for both scores to help AC create consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: As you assess reproducibility, think about not just whether the raw information to reproduce the paper are included, but how easy it would be to reproduce: imagine instructing someone with a strong CS/linguistics background how to reproduce the paper by e-mail using only the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you couldn't reproduce the work from the submission without a long clarifying e-mail, note what is missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report confidence level
rubrics_metrics.description: If your confidence is low, use the confidential comments section at the end of the form to let your meta-reviewer know which aspects of your review might not be reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the confidence marker to contextualize your review (and if you flag expertise gaps earlier, contact area chair).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and flags
rubrics_metrics.description: The review form allows you to flag the paper for potential breaches of ACL’s anonymity period, or indicate that you know the authors’ identity from some source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you notice deanonymization (self-citations, acknowledgements, non-anonymous repos), contact senior area chair early so they can adjust assignments or consider desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Paper nomination guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering a Best Paper nomination, think how you could argue this will be a best paper rather than whether it is already perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider potential, uniqueness of topic/technique, and how you'd argue it could be Best Paper after improvements; be less conservative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag issues with specific, understandable statements so an area chair can evaluate without searching the submission; prefer concrete examples over vague claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the document show bad vs good phrasing (e.g., 'The paper is missing relevant references' -> 'The paper is missing references XYZ'). Specificity helps chairs and authors address concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shortcut heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on quick heuristics (e.g., 'not SOTA', 'results not surprising', 'too simple', 'not novel', 'topic too niche', 'doesn't use my preferred methodology') as a reason to dismiss papers without further analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists common heuristics and explains why each can be problematic; if you use such a heuristic, back it up with arguments and references. Missing references are a problem only if the work was published 3+ months before deadline per ACL policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check scores match text
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that your numeric scores (especially Soundness) are justified by the criticisms in your review text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low soundness must be backed up with serious objections; excitement is subjective but should also have textual justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professional, neutral tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind; avoid rudeness, sarcasm, or demeaning language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the review you would like to receive; consider authors' career stage and mental health; be constructive and respectful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update review after author response and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: After the author response and reviewer discussion, update your review and scores if your opinion changed; explain why changes occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors often feel ignored if reviews don't change; even if unchanged, add a line saying what you found convincing or not. If you dramatically change a score, explain because chairs won't see discussion on the submission site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of review issues authors may flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can flag reviews for specific types of low-quality behavior: A) not specific enough; B) heuristics/shortcuts used without diligence; C) scores not matching text; D) rude/unprofessional; E) lack of expertise; F) mismatch with paper type; G) mismatch with contribution type; H) missing or too short and uninformative review; I) late review; J) other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism is for serious issues only; authors should explain which reviewer and why using a short template (250 words max).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible NLP checklist — A. For every submission
rubrics_metrics.description: A1. Did you describe the limitations of your work? A2. Did you discuss any potential risks of your work? A3. Do the abstract and introduction summarize the paper’s main claims? A4. Did you use AI writing assistants when working on this paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This checklist is visible to reviewers and can be used as a FAQ to see if authors already answered common reproducibility/ethics questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible NLP checklist — B. Artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used? B2. Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution of any artifacts? B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifact(s) was consistent with intended use (and specify intended use for created artifacts)? B4. Did you discuss steps taken to check if data contains identifiable/offensive content and steps taken to protect/anonymize it? B5. Did you provide documentation of artifacts (coverage of domains, languages, phenomena, demographics)? B6. Did you report relevant statistics like number of examples and train/test/dev splits?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers can treat these answers as a FAQ before asking checklist-scoped questions in their reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible NLP checklist — C. Computational experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: C1. Did you report the number of parameters in the models used, total computational budget (e.g., GPU hours), and computing infrastructure? C2. Did you discuss experimental setup, including hyperparameter search and best-found values? C3. Did you report descriptive statistics about results (error bars, summary stats, whether reporting max/mean/single run)? C4. If using existing packages, did you report implementation, model, and parameter settings used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items guide reproducibility and honest reporting of computational experiments; check both inclusion and sufficiency of details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible NLP checklist — D. Human annotators / human participants
rubrics_metrics.description: D1. Did you report full text of instructions given to participants? D2. Did you report how you recruited and paid participants and discuss payment adequacy? D3. Did you discuss how consent was obtained for data used/curated? D4. Was the data collection protocol approved (or exempt) by an ethics review board? D5. Did you report basic demographic and geographic characteristics of the annotator population?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items relate to ethics and fairness in human-subjects research; reviewers should check answers and flag ethics review if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics review referral criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: General PC members are not expected to be ethics experts. If you see something potentially problematic (data set collection issues, potential abuse, disadvantages for minority groups), you can flag the paper to be reviewed by a dedicated ethics review team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack expertise but suspect a serious ethical issue, flag for the ACL ethics committee who will recommend accept/revise/reject on ethical grounds. Uphold ACM Code of Ethics principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to tell if authors' Responsible NLP answers are satisfactory
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single number for 'fair pay' or 'legal grounds'—practices differ by country/institution. Authors must make their case and convince reviewers that their decisions were appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you think there's a serious ethical issue but lack expertise, flag for separate ethics review rather than making unilateral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI writing assistants for reviews (FAQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: It could be reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review or help non-native speakers; tools that check proofs or explain concepts may be reasonable as long as they don't mislead the reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because submissions and reviews are confidential and some tools (e.g., ChatGPT) may retain data, the use of non-privacy-friendly solutions for peer review is highly discouraged.
